summary: Qualitative breakdown of all 16 errors the abstaining qwen2.5:7b judge makes on the 120 cases it chooses to answer (200-case benchmark). Not all 16 are the same kind of mistake, and one isn't a model error at all.

A_overliteral_on_trivial_year_mismatch.description: Title matches exactly (often verbatim, read aloud by the speaker) except the spoken year differs from LIMS's recorded year by one -- a known, harmless DC legislative-calendar quirk the model doesn't know to discount.
examples: supported_pool#18 (Langston Slater Act, 2026 spoken vs 2025 recorded)
supported_pool#53 (Deferred Retirement Option Program Act, same pattern)

B_missed_substantive_connection.description: The real content clearly supports the title's actual subject, but doesn't share enough literal words with it for the model to connect them -- synonyms, domain acronyms (BSA, a term the model should plausibly know but didn't apply here), or a description one inferential step removed from the title's exact phrasing.
examples: weak_pool#12, #13, #37 (property appeals, names read in a list)

C_overconfident_on_empty_content.description: The MOST CONCERNING category: the model said 'contradicted' with no real content to judge at all -- pure procedural text ('all those in favor say aye'). This is the opposite failure mode from the headline abstention story: here the model manufactured confidence instead of abstaining, on cases that should have been the easiest to correctly flag as unverifiable.
examples: no_context_pool#43 (literally just a vote, zero description)

D_genuine_ambiguous_edge_case.description: Not clearly an error either direction: the speaker says the bill is 'now entitled' a different name than LIMS has on file, consistent with a genuine mid-session rename the LIMS snapshot predates.
examples: supported_pool#27 (Alma W. Thomas vs. Dolores Tucker Middle School)

E_benign_name_transcription_variant.description: Same person, phonetically-close CART transcription spelling (a pattern independently confirmed 4+ times across the full benchmark) -- treated as a mismatch when it's a transcription artifact, not a real content disagreement.

F_not_a_model_error_methodology_artifact.description: The one case where the LLM called a synthetic negative 'supported' is not a model mistake: the randomly swapped title coincidentally matches an ADJACENT citation's content that's genuinely present in the same context window (multiple citations read in sequence). Confirmed in isolation -- only 1 of 50 synthetic negatives has this property, and it's exactly this one.
examples: synthetic_contradicted#24 (Paul Goldstein, Board of Zoning Adjustment)

takeaway: Roughly 70% of errors (A+B) are the model being too conservative/literal on cases that were actually fine -- consistent with and reinforcing the project's overall finding that this approach fails safe. About 19% (C) are a genuinely concerning overconfidence failure worth flagging prominently, not burying in the aggregate error rate. One error is a defensible edge case, one is a transcription artifact, and one isn't a real error at all.
